title: Book 4, Chapter 13 — Seventh and Eighth Years of the War—End of Corcyraean Revolution— Peace of Gela—Capture of Nisaea
paragraphs: The same summer, directly after these events, the Athenians launched an expedition against Corinthian territory. They had eighty ships, two thousand Athenian heavy infantry, and two hundred cavalry carried on horse transports, with the Milesians, Andrians and Carystians of the allies in support. Nicias, son of Niceratus, commanded, with two colleagues. They put out to sea and at daybreak landed between Chersonese and Rheitus, on the beach below the Solygian hill. In old times the Dorians had settled on that hill and made war from it on the Aeolian inhabitants of Corinth, and a village called Solygia stands there now. The beach where the fleet came in is about a mile and a half from the village, seven miles from Corinth, and two and a quarter from the Isthmus. The Corinthians had heard from Argos that the Athenian armament was coming, and long before had gathered at the Isthmus, all except those who lived beyond it and five hundred who were away as garrison in Ambracia and Leucadia. They were there in full force, watching for the Athenians to land. But the Athenians slipped past them by arriving in the dark. The Corinthians were told by signals, left half their number at Cenchreae in case the Athenians should go against Crommyon, and marched in all haste to meet the landing.

Battus, one of the two generals present at the action, took a company to defend the village of Solygia, which had no fortifications, while Lycophron stayed to give battle with the rest. The Corinthians first attacked the Athenian right wing, which had just landed in front of Chersonese, and then the rest of the army. The battle was stubborn and was fought hand to hand throughout. The Athenians and Carystians of the right wing, who had been placed at the end of the line, withstood the Corinthians and with some difficulty drove them back. The Corinthians retreated to a wall on the rising ground behind, threw stones down on their enemies, and then came on again singing the paean. The Athenians received them, and they were again engaged at close quarters. At this moment a Corinthian company came to the relief of the left wing, routed the Athenian right and chased it down to the sea. From the ships, however, the Athenians and Carystians drove the Corinthians back in their turn. Meanwhile the rest of the army on either side fought on tenaciously, above all the Corinthian right wing, where Lycophron held out against the Athenian left. It was feared that this left might make an attempt on the village of Solygia.

For a long time neither side gave way. Then the Athenians, helped by their cavalry (the enemy had none), at length routed the Corinthians, who withdrew to the hill and halted there, and did not come down again. It was in this rout of their right wing that they lost the most men, and Lycophron their general was among the dead. The rest of the army was broken and put to flight in the same way, but without being seriously pursued or pressed, and it retired to the high ground and took up its position there. The Athenians saw that the enemy no longer offered battle. They stripped his dead, took up their own, and immediately set up a trophy. Meanwhile the half of the Corinthians who had been left at Cenchreae to guard against an Athenian landing at Crommyon could not see the battle because of Mount Oneion, but learned what was happening from the dust and hurried to the rescue. So did the older Corinthians from the town, when they discovered what had occurred. The Athenians saw them all coming against them and thought they were reinforcements arriving from the neighboring Peloponnesians. They withdrew in haste to their ships with their spoils and their own dead, except two whom they could not find and so left behind. They went on board and crossed over to the islands opposite, and from there sent a herald and recovered under truce the bodies they had left. Two hundred and twelve Corinthians fell in the battle, and rather fewer than fifty Athenians.

The Athenians weighed anchor from the islands and sailed the same day to Crommyon in Corinthian territory, about thirteen miles from the city. They anchored there, laid waste the country, and spent the night. The next day they first coasted along to the territory of Epidaurus and made a landing there. Then they came to Methana, between Epidaurus and Troezen, and drew a wall across the isthmus of the peninsula and fortified it. They left a post there, from which raids were afterwards made on the country of Troezen, Haliae and Epidaurus. When they had walled off this spot, the fleet sailed home.

While these events were going on, Eurymedon and Sophocles had put to sea with the Athenian fleet from Pylos on their way to Sicily. They arrived at Corcyra and joined the townsmen in an expedition against the party established on Mount Istone. As I have mentioned, this party had crossed over after the revolution and become masters of the country, to the great harm of the inhabitants. Their stronghold was taken by assault, and the garrison took refuge in a body on some high ground and capitulated there. They agreed to give up their mercenary auxiliaries, to lay down their arms, and to submit themselves to the discretion of the Athenian people. The generals carried them across under truce to the island of Ptychia, to be held in custody until they could be sent to Athens. It was agreed that if any of them were caught trying to escape, all would lose the benefit of the treaty. Meanwhile the leaders of the Corcyraean commons were afraid that the Athenians might spare the lives of the prisoners, and they resorted to the following stratagem. They won over a few of the men on the island by secretly sending friends to them, with instructions to provide them with a boat and to tell them, as if for their own sakes, that they had best escape as quickly as possible, since the Athenian generals were going to hand them over to the Corcyraean people.

These representations succeeded. It was arranged that the men were caught sailing out in the boat that had been provided, and so the treaty became void and the whole body was handed over to the Corcyraeans. The Athenian generals were in great part responsible for this result. They plainly did not want to sail for Sicily, and so leave to others the honor of conducting the men to Athens. This encouraged the intriguers in their design and seemed to confirm what they had told the prisoners. The Corcyraeans shut up the prisoners thus handed over in a large building. Afterwards they took them out by twenties, bound together, and led them past two lines of heavy infantry, one on each side. The men in the lines beat and stabbed any prisoner they saw to be a personal enemy, while men carrying whips walked beside the column and hurried along those who went too slowly.

As many as sixty men were taken out and killed in this way without the knowledge of their friends in the building, who fancied they were merely being moved from one prison to another. At last, however, someone opened their eyes to the truth. They then called on the Athenians to kill them themselves, if that was their pleasure, refused to go out of the building any longer, and said they would do all they could to prevent anyone coming in. The Corcyraeans did not wish to force a passage through the doors themselves. They climbed on top of the building, broke through the roof, threw down the tiles, and shot arrows at the prisoners, who sheltered from them as well as they could. Most of the prisoners, meanwhile, were busy killing themselves, driving into their throats the arrows shot by the enemy, and hanging themselves with cords taken from some beds that happened to be there and with strips torn from their clothing. In short, they adopted every possible means of self-destruction, and they also fell victim to the missiles of their enemies on the roof. Night came on while these horrors were being enacted, and most of it had passed before they were over. When it was day, the Corcyraeans threw the bodies in layers onto wagons and carried them out of the city. All the women taken in the stronghold were sold as slaves. In this way the Corcyraeans of the mountain were destroyed by the commons. And so, after terrible excesses, the party strife came to an end, at least as far as the period of this war is concerned, for of one party there was practically nothing left. Meanwhile the Athenians sailed off to Sicily, their original destination, and carried on the war there with their allies.

At the close of the summer, the Athenians at Naupactus and the Acarnanians made an expedition against Anactorium, the Corinthian town at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, and took it by treachery. The Acarnanians themselves then sent settlers from all parts of Acarnania and occupied the place.

Summer was now over. During the winter that followed, Aristides, son of Archippus, who was one of the commanders of the Athenian ships sent to collect money from the allies, arrested a Persian named Artaphernes at Eion, on the Strymon. Artaphernes was on his way from the King to Lacedaemon. He was taken to Athens, where the Athenians had his dispatches translated from the Assyrian script and read them. The letter touched on many other subjects, but in substance it told the Lacedaemonians that the King did not know what they wanted, since of the many ambassadors they had sent him no two ever told the same story. If, however, they were prepared to speak plainly, they might send him some envoys with this Persian. Afterwards the Athenians sent Artaphernes back to Ephesus in a galley, and ambassadors with him. There they heard of the death of King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, which had taken place about that time, and so they returned home.

The same winter the Chians pulled down their new wall at the command of the Athenians, who suspected them of planning an insurrection. They first obtained pledges from the Athenians, and such security as was possible, that they would go on being treated as before. Thus the winter ended, and with it ended the seventh year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

In the first days of the next summer there was an eclipse of the sun at the time of the new moon, and early in the same month an earthquake. Meanwhile the Mitylenian and other Lesbian exiles set out, mostly from the continent, with mercenaries hired in Peloponnese and others raised on the spot. They took Rhoeteum, but restored it undamaged on receiving two thousand Phocaean staters. After this they marched against Antandrus and took the town by treachery. Their plan was to free Antandrus and the rest of the Actaean towns, which had formerly belonged to Mitylene but were now held by the Athenians. Once fortified there, they would have every facility for building ships, since Ida was near and timber therefore plentiful, and plenty of other supplies besides. From this base they could easily ravage Lesbos, which was not far off, and make themselves masters of the Aeolian towns on the continent.

While the exiles were making these plans, the Athenians in the same summer made an expedition against Cythera with sixty ships, two thousand heavy infantry, a few cavalry, and some allied troops from Miletus and other places. The commanders were Nicias, son of Niceratus, Nicostratus, son of Diotrephes, and Autocles, son of Tolmaeus. Cythera is an island lying off Laconia, opposite Malea. Its inhabitants are Lacedaemonians of the class of the Perioeci, and an officer called the judge of Cythera went over to the place every year from Sparta. A garrison of heavy infantry was also regularly sent there, and great attention was paid to the island. It was the landing place for merchant ships from Egypt and Libya, and it also protected Laconia from raids by pirates from the sea at the only point where Laconia can be attacked, since the whole coast rises abruptly toward the Sicilian and Cretan seas.

The Athenians came to land with their armament. With ten ships and two thousand Milesian heavy infantry they took the town of Scandea, on the sea. With the rest of their forces they landed on the side of the island facing Malea and went against the lower town of Cythera, where they found all the inhabitants encamped. A battle followed. The Cytherians held their ground for a short while, then turned and fled into the upper town, and soon afterwards capitulated to Nicias and his colleagues. They agreed to leave their fate to the decision of the Athenians, with only their lives guaranteed. Nicias had previously been in correspondence with some of the inhabitants, and this made the surrender quicker and gave the Cytherians better terms, both then and later. Otherwise the Athenians would have expelled them, because they were Lacedaemonians and their island lay so near Laconia. After the capitulation the Athenians occupied the town of Scandea, near the harbor, and appointed a garrison for Cythera. They then sailed to Asine, Helus and most of the places on the sea, made landings, camped for the night on shore at convenient spots, and went on ravaging the country for about seven days.

The Lacedaemonians saw the Athenians masters of Cythera and expected landings of the same kind on their coasts. They nowhere opposed them in force, but sent garrisons here and there through the country, each made up of as many heavy infantry as the threatened points seemed to require, and for the most part kept strictly on the defensive. They had suffered a severe and unexpected blow on the island, Pylos and Cythera were occupied, and on every side they saw a war whose rapidity defied precaution. They lived in constant fear of internal revolution, and now took the unusual step of raising four hundred horse and a force of archers. They became more timid than ever in military matters, since they found themselves involved in a naval struggle, which their organization had never contemplated, and against Athenians, who always counted an enterprise left unattempted as a success thrown away. Besides this, their numerous recent reverses, coming one upon another without any reason, had thoroughly unnerved them. They were always afraid of a second disaster like that on the island, and so scarcely dared to take the field. They fancied that they could not make a move without a blunder, for they were new to the experience of adversity and had lost all confidence in themselves.

Accordingly they now let the Athenians ravage their seaboard without making any move. The garrison in whose neighborhood a landing was made always thought its numbers insufficient and shared the general feeling. A single garrison, near Cotyrta and Aphrodisia, did venture to resist. Its charge struck terror into the scattered mob of light troops, but when it was met by the heavy infantry it retreated, with the loss of a few men and some arms. The Athenians set up a trophy for this and then sailed off to Cythera. From there they sailed round to Epidaurus Limera, ravaged part of the country, and so came to Thyrea in the Cynurian territory, on the border between Argos and Laconia. The Lacedaemonians who owned this district had given it to the expelled Aeginetans to live in. They did so in return for the Aeginetans’ good services at the time of the earthquake and the rising of the Helots, and also because, although subjects of Athens, the Aeginetans had always sided with Lacedaemon.

While the Athenians were still at sea, the Aeginetans abandoned a fort they were building on the coast and retreated into the upper town where they lived, rather more than a mile from the sea. One of the Lacedaemonian district garrisons, which was helping them with the work, refused to enter the town with them, though they begged it to. It thought it dangerous to shut itself up within the wall, and it withdrew to the high ground and kept quiet, not considering itself a match for the enemy. Meanwhile the Athenians landed, advanced at once with all their forces, and took Thyrea. They burned the town and plundered what was in it. The Aeginetans who were not killed in the fighting they took with them to Athens, together with Tantalus, son of Patrocles, their Lacedaemonian commander, who had been wounded and taken prisoner. They also took with them a few men from Cythera whom they thought it safest to remove. The Athenians decided to lodge these in the islands. The rest of the Cytherians were to keep their lands and pay four talents tribute. The captured Aeginetans were all to be put to death, because of the old inveterate feud, and Tantalus was to share the imprisonment of the Lacedaemonians taken on the island.

The same summer, the inhabitants of Camarina and Gela in Sicily first made an armistice with each other. After this, embassies from all the other Sicilian cities assembled at Gela to try to bring about a pacification. Many opinions were expressed on one side and the other, according to the grievances and claims of the different parties. Then Hermocrates, son of Hermon, a Syracusan and the most influential man among them, addressed the assembly in these words:

“Sicilians, if I speak now, it is not because my city is the least in Sicily or the one that has suffered most from the war. I speak in order to state publicly what seems to me the best policy for the whole island. That war is an evil is so familiar to everyone that it would be tedious to argue it at length. No one is forced into war by ignorance, or kept out of it by fear, if he fancies there is something to be gained by it. To the first, the gain looks greater than the danger. The second would rather run the risk than put up with any immediate sacrifice. But if both should happen to have chosen the wrong moment for acting in this way, advice to make peace would not be unhelpful. And this, if we would only see it, is exactly what we most need at the present juncture.

“I suppose that no one will dispute that we went to war at first to serve our own separate interests, that we are now debating, in view of the same interests, how we can make peace, and that if we part without having what we think our rights, we shall go to war again. And yet, as men of sense, we ought to see that our separate interests are not the only thing at stake in this congress. There is also the question whether we still have time to save Sicily, the whole of which, in my opinion, is menaced by Athenian ambition. We ought to find in the very name of that people more compelling arguments for peace than any I can offer. We see the first power in Hellas watching our mistakes with the few ships she has at present in our waters. Under the fair name of alliance, she speciously seeks to turn to account the natural hostility that exists between us. Suppose we go to war and call in to help us a people who are ready enough to carry their arms even where they are not invited. Suppose we injure ourselves at our own expense and at the same time serve as the pioneers of their dominion. Then we may expect that when they see us worn out they will one day come with a larger armament and try to bring all of us into subjection.

“And yet, if we as sensible men call in allies and court danger, it should be to enrich our different countries with new acquisitions, and not to ruin what they already possess. We should understand that internal discord, which is so fatal to communities in general, will be equally fatal to Sicily if we, its inhabitants, absorbed in our local quarrels, neglect the common enemy. These considerations should reconcile individual with individual and city with city, and unite us in a common effort to save the whole of Sicily. Nor should anyone imagine that only the Dorians are enemies of Athens, while the Chalcidian race is secured by its Ionian blood. The attack in question is not inspired by hatred of one of two nationalities, but by a desire for the good things of Sicily, which belong to all of us in common. This is proved by the way Athens received the Chalcidian invitation. An ally who has never given them any assistance whatever at once receives from them almost more than the treaty entitles him to. That the Athenians should cherish this ambition and follow this policy is very excusable. I do not blame those who wish to rule, but those who are over-ready to serve. It is just as much in men’s nature to rule those who submit to them as it is to resist those who molest them. The one is no less invariable than the other. Meanwhile all who see these dangers and refuse to provide against them properly are mistaken, and so are those who have come here without having made up their minds that our first duty is to unite to be rid of the common peril. The quickest way to be rid of it is to make peace with each other, since the Athenians menace us not from their own country but from the country of those who invited them here. In this way, instead of war issuing in war, peace quietly ends our quarrels. And the guests who come here under fair pretenses for bad ends will have good reason to go away without having attained them.

“So far as the Athenians are concerned, such are the great advantages shown to lie in a wise policy. Apart from this, there is the universal agreement that peace is the first of blessings. How then can we refuse to make it among ourselves? Or do you not think that the good you have, and the ills you complain of, would be better preserved and cured by quiet than by war? Peace has its honors and splendors, less perilous than those of war, not to mention the many other blessings one might dwell on, as one might dwell on the equally many miseries of war. These considerations should teach you not to disregard my words, but rather to look in them, each of you, for his own safety. Suppose there is anyone here who feels certain, whether by right or by might, of achieving his object. Let him not find this surprise too severe a disappointment. Let him remember that many before now have tried to chastise a wrongdoer and, failing to punish their enemy, have not even saved themselves. And many who have trusted in force to gain an advantage have, instead of gaining anything more, been doomed to lose what they had. Vengeance is not necessarily successful because wrong has been done, nor is strength sure because it is confident. The incalculable element in the future exercises the widest influence. It is the most treacherous of all things, and yet in fact the most useful, since it frightens us all equally and so makes us think before we attack each other.

“Let us therefore now allow the undefined fear of this unknown future, and the immediate terror of the Athenians’ presence, to have their natural effect. Let us regard any failure to carry out the programs that we may each have sketched out for ourselves as sufficiently accounted for by these obstacles, and let us send the intruder away from the country. If everlasting peace is impossible between us, let us at all events make a treaty for as long a term as possible, and put off our private differences to another day. In short, let us recognize that if we adopt my advice we shall each remain citizens of a free state, and as such arbiters of our own destiny, able to return good or bad offices with equal effect. If we reject it, we shall depend on others. We shall then be not only powerless to repel an insult, but, on the most favorable supposition, friends to our direst enemies and at feud with our natural friends.

“For myself, though, as I said at first, I represent a great city and am able to think less of defending myself than of attacking others, I am prepared to concede something in anticipation of these dangers. I am not inclined to ruin myself for the sake of hurting my enemies, nor so blinded by animosity as to think myself as much master of fortune, which I cannot command, as I am of my own plans. But I am ready to give up anything reasonable. I call upon the rest of you to follow my example of your own free will, without being forced to it by the enemy. There is no disgrace in kinsmen giving way to one another, a Dorian to a Dorian, or a Chalcidian to his brethren. Beyond this, we are neighbors, we live in the same country, we are girt by the same sea, and we go by the same name of Sicilians. We shall go to war again, I suppose, when the time comes, and again make peace among ourselves by means of future congresses. But the foreign invader, if we are wise, will always find us united against him, since the hurt of one is the danger of all. And we shall never in future invite into the island either allies or mediators. By so acting we shall at the present moment do Sicily a double service, ridding her at once of the Athenians and of civil war, and in future we shall live in freedom at home and be less menaced from abroad.”

Such were the words of Hermocrates. The Sicilians took his advice and came to an understanding among themselves to end the war, each keeping what they had. The Camarinaeans were to take Morgantina at a price fixed to be paid to the Syracusans. The allies of the Athenians then called the commanding officers and told them that they were going to make peace and that they would be included in the treaty. The generals assented, the peace was concluded, and the Athenian fleet afterwards sailed away from Sicily. When the generals arrived at Athens, the Athenians banished Pythodorus and Sophocles, and fined Eurymedon, for having taken bribes to depart when they might have subdued Sicily. So thoroughly had their present prosperity persuaded the citizens that nothing could withstand them, and that they could achieve what was possible and impracticable alike, whether their means were ample or inadequate. The secret of this was their general extraordinary success, which made them confuse their strength with their hopes.

The same summer the Megarians in the city were pressed by the hostilities of the Athenians, who invaded their country twice every year with all their forces. They were also harassed by the raids of their own exiles at Pegae, who had been expelled in a revolution by the popular party. They began to ask each other whether it would not be better to receive back their exiles and so free the town from one of its two scourges. The friends of the exiles saw the agitation and now demanded this proposal more openly than before. The leaders of the commons saw that the sufferings of the times had worn out the constancy of their supporters. In their alarm they entered into correspondence with the Athenian generals, Hippocrates, son of Ariphron, and Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and resolved to betray the town, thinking this less dangerous to themselves than the return of the party they had banished. It was accordingly arranged that the Athenians should first take the long walls, which extend for nearly a mile from the city to the port of Nisaea. This was to prevent the Peloponnesians coming to the rescue from Nisaea, where they were the sole garrison securing the fidelity of Megara. After this, an attempt was to be made to put the upper town into their hands, which it was thought would then come over with less difficulty.

Plans had been settled between the Athenians and their correspondents, both for what was to be said and for what was to be done. The Athenians then sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under Hippocrates, and took post in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be dug for the walls. Demosthenes, the other commander, placed himself in ambush with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it that night except those whose business it was to know. A little before daybreak the traitors in Megara began to act. For a long time they had been in the habit, every night, of carrying a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and sailing out in it, under pretense of marauding. This gave them a means of opening the gates, and they did it with the consent of the officer in command. They brought the boat back on the cart before day and took it inside the wall through the gates. Their pretended aim was to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbor. On this occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat. The Athenians, who had agreed on this with the traitors, saw it and ran from the ambush at top speed, to reach the gates before they were shut again and while the cart was still there to keep them from closing. At the same moment their Megarian accomplices killed the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, at the very spot where the trophy now stands. He was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and so secured the gates for the Athenian heavy infantry coming up.

After this, each of the Athenians, as fast as he entered, went against the wall. A few of the Peloponnesian garrison at first stood their ground and tried to repel the assault, and some of them were killed. But the main body took fright and fled. The night attack, and the sight of the Megarian traitors in arms against them, made them think that all Megara had gone over to the enemy. It also happened that the Athenian herald, on his own idea, called out and invited any Megarians who wished to join the Athenian ranks. The garrison no sooner heard this than they gave way. Convinced that they were the victims of a concerted attack, they took refuge in Nisaea. By daybreak the walls were taken and the Megarians in the city were in great agitation. The persons who had negotiated with the Athenians, supported by the rest of the popular party, which was privy to the plot, then said that the gates ought to be opened and the people should march out to battle. It had been agreed between them that the Athenians should rush in the moment the gates were opened, while the conspirators would be distinguished from the rest by being anointed with oil, so as to avoid being hurt. They could open the gates with more security because four thousand Athenian heavy infantry from Eleusis and six hundred horse had marched all night, according to the agreement, and were now close at hand. The conspirators were all anointed and at their posts by the gates, when one of their accomplices denounced the plot to the opposite party. These gathered together and came in a body. They said bluntly that the people must not march out, a thing they had never yet ventured even when in greater force than at present, nor wantonly compromise the safety of the town, and that if their advice was not heeded, the battle would have to be fought in Megara itself. For the rest, they gave no sign that they knew of the intrigue, but stoutly maintained that their advice was the best. Meanwhile they kept close by and watched the gates, which made it impossible for the conspirators to carry out their purpose.

The Athenian generals saw that some obstacle had arisen and that taking the town by force was no longer practicable. They at once proceeded to invest Nisaea, thinking that if they could take it before relief arrived, the surrender of Megara would soon follow. Iron, stone-masons and everything else required came up quickly from Athens. Starting from the wall they occupied, the Athenians built a cross wall facing Megara, down to the sea on either side of Nisaea. The ditch and the walls were divided among the army. Stones and bricks were taken from the suburb, and the fruit-trees and timber were cut down to make a palisade wherever one seemed necessary. The houses in the suburb, with battlements added, sometimes also became part of the fortification. The work continued the whole of that day, and by the afternoon of the next the wall was all but complete. Then the garrison in Nisaea capitulated to the Athenians. They were alarmed by their complete lack of provisions, which they had been used to take in for the day from the upper town. They did not expect any speedy relief from the Peloponnesians, and they supposed Megara to be hostile. The condition was that they should give up their arms and each be ransomed for a stipulated sum, while their Lacedaemonian commander, and any others of his countrymen in the place, were left to the discretion of the Athenians. On these conditions they surrendered and came out. The Athenians broke down the long walls at their point of junction with Megara, took possession of Nisaea, and went on with their other preparations.

Just at this time the Lacedaemonian Brasidas, son of Tellis, happened to be in the neighborhood of Sicyon and Corinth, getting ready an army for Thrace. As soon as he heard that the walls had been taken, he feared for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and for the safety of Megara. He sent to the Boeotians to meet him as quickly as possible at Tripodiscus, a village of the Megarid so called, under Mount Geraneia. He went there himself with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian heavy infantry, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and such troops of his own as he had already levied, expecting to find Nisaea not yet taken. Hearing of its fall (he had marched out by night to Tripodiscus), he took three hundred picked men from the army without waiting until his coming should be known, and came up to Megara unobserved by the Athenians, who were down by the sea. His purpose was, ostensibly, and really if possible, to make an attempt on Nisaea, but above all to get into Megara and secure the town. He accordingly invited the townspeople to admit his party, saying that he had hopes of recovering Nisaea.

However, one of the Megarian factions feared that he might expel them and restore the exiles. The other feared that the commons, apprehensive of this very danger, might set upon them, and that the city would then be destroyed by a battle within its gates, under the eyes of the Athenians lying in ambush. He was accordingly refused admittance. Both parties chose to remain quiet and await the event, each expecting a battle between the Athenians and the relieving army, and each thinking it safer to see its friends victorious before declaring in their favor.

Unable to carry his point, Brasidas went back to the rest of the army. At daybreak the Boeotians joined him. They had determined to relieve Megara, whose danger they considered their own, even before hearing from Brasidas, and were already in full force at Plataea when his messenger arrived to add spurs to their resolution. They at once sent on to him two thousand two hundred heavy infantry and six hundred horse, and returned home with the main body. The whole army thus assembled numbered six thousand heavy infantry. The Athenian heavy infantry were drawn up by Nisaea and the sea. But their light troops were scattered over the plain, and the Boeotian horse attacked them and drove them to the sea. They were taken entirely by surprise, since on previous occasions no relief had ever come to the Megarians from any quarter. Here the Boeotians were in their turn charged and engaged by the Athenian horse, and a cavalry action followed which lasted a long time, and in which both parties claimed the victory. The Athenians killed and stripped the leader of the Boeotian horse, together with a few of his comrades who had charged right up to Nisaea. They remained masters of the bodies, gave them back under truce, and set up a trophy. But in the action as a whole the forces separated without either side having gained a decisive advantage, the Boeotians returning to their army and the Athenians to Nisaea.

After this Brasidas and the army came nearer to the sea and to Megara. They took up a convenient position and remained quiet in order of battle, expecting to be attacked by the Athenians and knowing that the Megarians were waiting to see which side would be the victor. This attitude seemed to offer two advantages. They did not take the offensive or willingly provoke the hazards of a battle, yet they openly showed their readiness to fight, and so would fairly reap the honors of the day without bearing its burden. At the same time they effectively served their interests at Megara. For if they had failed to show themselves, they would not have had a chance, but would certainly have been considered vanquished and would have lost the town. As it was, the Athenians might possibly not be inclined to accept their challenge, and their object would be attained without fighting. And so it turned out. The Athenians formed outside the long walls and, since the enemy did not attack, stood there motionless. Their generals had decided that the risk was too unequal. In fact most of their objects had already been attained. They would have to begin a battle against superior numbers, and if victorious could only gain Megara, while a defeat would destroy the flower of their heavy soldiery. For the enemy it was different. Even the states actually represented in his army each risked only a part of its entire force, so he might well be more audacious. Accordingly, after waiting for some time without either side attacking, the Athenians withdrew to Nisaea, and the Peloponnesians after them to the point from which they had set out. The friends of the Megarian exiles now threw aside their hesitation. They looked upon Brasidas as the victor and upon the Athenians as having declined the battle, and so they opened the gates to him and to the commanders from the different states, received them into the town and proceeded to discuss matters with them. The party in correspondence with the Athenians was paralyzed by the turn things had taken.

Afterwards Brasidas let the allies go home and went back himself to Corinth, to prepare for his expedition to Thrace, his original destination. The Athenians also returned home. The Megarians in the city who were most implicated in the Athenian negotiation knew that they had been detected, and presently disappeared. The rest conferred with the friends of the exiles and restored the party at Pegae, after binding them under solemn oaths to take no vengeance for the past and only to consult the real interests of the town. However, as soon as these men were in office, they held a review of the heavy infantry. They separated the battalions and picked out about a hundred of their enemies, those thought to be most involved in the correspondence with the Athenians. They brought them before the people and compelled the vote to be given openly, and had them condemned and executed, and established a close oligarchy in the town. This revolution lasted a very long while, although effected by a very few partisans.
